newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam says ailing president simply "tired".
newsitem.headline: Vietnam says ailing president simply "tired".

text.p: Vietnam broke an official silence over the health of President Le Duc Anh on Monday, responding to reports that the 75-year-old general had suffered a stroke with a brief explanation that he was tired and needed rest.
"What we know is that President Le Duc Anh is tired and, as requested by doctors, he needs a rest," a foreign ministry spokesman said in a statement.

Political and diplomatic sources said Anh, a member of the communist country's leadership triumvirate, was paralysed down one side by an apoplexy. They said doctors were not optimistic that he would recover sufficiently to resume his presidential duties.
One source, who declined to be named, said the president had regained consciousness in Hanoi's 108 Army hospital on Sunday and had already asked to be allowed to return to work.
"He regained consciousness and...started recognising people. But he is half-paralysed and will be out of his post," the source said.
Under the constitution, when the country's president is incapacitated for work "over a long period of time" the vice-president, currently Nguyen Thi Binh, must act in his place.

If the post falls vacant, the vice-president must stand in until the election of a new president by the National Assembly. The assembly's next session is not due until March or April, but an extraordinary session could be convened.
The country's state-controlled media made no mention of Anh's illness and even reported that he had sent greetings to the president of Latvia and the head of state of Oman on Sunday.
The Foreign Ministry spokesman said Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi would receive South Korea's President Kim Young-sam, whom Anh had invited for an official visit to Hanoi later this week.

Anh is a key figure in the country's leadership triumvirate, a collective system comprising three powerful figures chosen to ensure balance between different shades of socialist opinion and differing regional views.
The other members of the trio are party chief Muoi, 79, who is seen as occupying a central and stabilising role in government, and the reformist Prime Minister, Vo Van Kiet, 73.

Anh, viewed by Western observers as the most conservative of the three, played key roles in independence struggles against the French and then the Americans, in the 1978 invasion of Cambodia and, finally, in normalising ties with China in 1991.
As president, he is also seen as an essential part of the mechanism by which close party-army ties are ensured.
Diplomats say the impact of his possible departure from the political scene would depend largely on the choice of successor.
The next most senior member of the Politburo below Anh, and with a military background, is Lieutenant-General Le Kha Phieu, 64.

However, diplomats believe that there is no obvious successor and said other senior Politburo members, not necessarily military personnel, would be in the running to fill Anh's post if it became vacant.
